questions.q: Which category of GPU memory usage during training typically scales with batch size and is usually what causes an out-of-memory error first?
options: Model parameters
Optimizer state
Activations — the intermediate tensors saved during the forward pass for use in backward
The CUDA driver itself
questions.explain: Activations scale directly with batch size and sequence length, making them the category most likely to exceed available memory first.

questions.q: In a `torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError` message, what is the difference between 'allocated' and 'reserved but unallocated' memory?
options: There is no difference; they mean the same thing
Allocated memory is actively backing live tensors; reserved-but-unallocated memory is cached by PyTorch's allocator for reuse but not currently holding a tensor
Allocated memory is on the CPU; reserved memory is on the GPU
Reserved memory is memory that has been permanently lost to fragmentation
questions.explain: PyTorch's allocator distinguishes memory currently backing tensors (allocated) from memory it has cached for future reuse but isn't using right now (reserved).

questions.q: Why does `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` usually fail to fix a genuine out-of-memory problem?
options: It only works on CPU tensors
It releases cached-but-unallocated memory back to the driver, but does nothing for memory that your own tensors are actively holding
It increases the model's batch size automatically
It permanently disables the GPU
questions.explain: empty_cache() frees memory PyTorch had cached for reuse, not memory currently in use by live tensors — so it doesn't help if the model genuinely needs more memory than available.

questions.q: How does gradient checkpointing reduce memory usage?
options: It stores all activations in a compressed format
It discards intermediate activations during the forward pass and recomputes them during backward, trading extra compute time for less memory
It reduces the number of layers in the model
It moves the optimizer state to CPU memory permanently
questions.explain: Gradient checkpointing avoids storing every intermediate activation by recomputing them as needed during backpropagation, reducing peak memory at the cost of extra compute.

questions.q: How does gradient accumulation let you reach a larger effective batch size without more memory?
options: By running several smaller forward/backward passes and summing their gradients before a single optimizer step, instead of one large pass
By compressing the model's weights to a lower precision
By disabling the optimizer's momentum terms
By splitting the model across multiple GPUs automatically
questions.explain: Gradient accumulation processes several smaller batches, summing their gradients, before applying one optimizer step — achieving the same effective batch size with only a fraction of the activation memory held at once.
